Derek Watts – The People’s Presenter

Part 1 Duration: 12 min 07 12 Frames ( without the handles)

Claire; I remember it was one of my first times in studio and at the end of my first show he turned to me and he gave me a fist bump and he looked me in the eye and it was all right with the world

Mac: His smile, and that hand you know when ever you meet Derek he will greet you and he will always put his hand on your shoulder and I think no matter how bad your day was that comforting big hand on your shoulder makes you feel like everything is going to be ok.

Masa: He used to make me laugh so much. He gave me really good advice. I will miss hearing his footsteps in the corridor, you can hear Derek’s footsteps he’s what 2 metres tall… I will miss hearing his footsteps because I know what comes after those footsteps, good energy.

Mac: He has touched my life in an incredible way. He gave his all and his heart to everyone that he met.

“Derek, take let’s go we can’t wait ..lets go“
Derek: You’re not serious…. You b…. keep me going the whole time…. Judging by the bleary eyes we saw at the conference yesterday, you guys have had mornings like this every morning so far.

V/O
The people’s presenter, Derek Watts entered our living rooms and our lives over 40 years ago.

UP SOUND
“I feel like kissing you”
Derek: My lucky night guys

V/O
For most of that time he was on Carte Blanche’s screen as anchor and journalist, something in his own words he felt extremely proud of. And we as his Carte Blanche family - past and present – are grateful that Derek touched each and every one of us, in his own special way. This is our tribute.

Derek: Its 7pm I’m Derek Watts and this is Carte Blanche

George As a journalist he has to have had probably the longest career of any broadcast journalist certainly on the African continent if not globally.

Claire: He’s been the fabric of story telling, for as far back as I remember I remember.

Derek and Ruda on screen: Hello and welcome to the last Carte Blanche of 1993

Claire: Sunday night and I would be sitting on the floor dreading the fact that I would have to go to school tomorrow and my mother would tell us keep quiet Derek and Ruda are on and its serious news.


Devi: I watched the very first episode of CB when I was 15 years old I knew that in order to prepare for this CB interview which I would one day do in my head, I would audition for the show. I watched his every single move, I had this little book where I would write notes because for me it served as almost a text book of what existed and how it should be done. So I knew Derek as a fan just like millions of other South Africans.

V/O
Derek Neil Watts was born in 1948, in Hillbrow, Johannesburg. He was the youngest of three, behind his brother Roy and sister Gaynor.

Mac: He was Mr Carte Blanche right. ..we always looked at CB that’s the ultimate, that’s the holy grail.

Masa: People want to share their stories people want to rell their deepest darkest secrets

V/O
Derek’s father Basil, a fitter and turner, was a disarmingly honest man with a hatred of lies. His mother, Edna, would entertain friends with her piano playing and a few risqué routines. Qualities Derek inherited - an ability to capture an audience and an abhorrence of dishonesty.

Derek: Dennis hey,
‘That’s right’
Derek: Derek’s my name from Carte Blanche, Dennis you try and sell courses for R150 00 for one course. What was he going to get out of it?
‘That’s irrelevant’

V/O
The family moved to Bulawayo in what was then Rhodesia. Derek was an easy-going boy who loved reading … he was also, naughty, an out-and-out rebel.

Claire: Fun was at the centre of a lot of what he would be doing so it looks very serious broadcasting live to the nation in the studio but there are little cheeky dad jokes that are creeping in. He’s making fun of camera crew he’s having a good time you can imagine what Derek was like as a teenager….

V/O
Laid back, personal, hugely curious, Derek was not a great success as a student at Natal University. It was not the endless party he’d envisaged.

Mac: It’s the naughtiness, he’s got a very wicked sense of humour

Penthouse Link
There are 15 international versions of Penthouse magazine and its been my duty as a Carte Blanche reporter to flip through most of them.
V/O
His father thought the army would sort him out and in a sense it did. He was selected for the Officers Training Course, ending up as a company commander in the Rhodesian Bush war - or the Zimbabwean Liberation War - depending on whose side you were. A long and bitter conflict.

UPSOUND:DEREK WATTS
DEREK: There was a lot of propaganda, we know that [...] we’d been told we were fighting against CT’s – Communist Terrorists, but you know, the truth was different wasn’t it? I mean it was a liberation struggle and I think in the back of our minds, yeah, we knew that was really what it was about.
But in the end, many people lost their lives.
I think by ’78, I’d lost that initial belief in what we were fighting for.

V/O
It’s in the in the army that key characteristics of the Derek identity came to the fore - so evident in some of his tougher assignments.

SFX Floris breathe

John: There is the famous story the story I don’t know if it’s become urban legend or its been embellished. But the story that he did in the Balkans during that terrible war in Bosnia in the early 90s when he travelled to cover this amazing British woman… and he arrived in Mostar, a town at the centre of this conflict and did a piece to camera in what he thought was just an arbitrary road and he was informed by the locals later that it was snipers alley and that he could have been shot at any time.

Derek: In this area hardly a building has been left intact, there’s a putrid smell in the air you can only imagine how much blood has been split how many lives have been lost, how many families obliterated in this street alone.

V/O
Working as a cadet reporter for the Rhodesian Herald - in between his army postings - Derek became very disillusioned. The Smith government’s censorship prevented journalists reporting on what was really happening in the country.

Masa: Derek Watts, He is Power to Truth he is a social Justice Warrior He was just this ginormous larger than life person who walked into the room and just owned it but there was just so much light and warmth…I think I may have been just little bit star struck in the beginning but who isn’t when they meet Derek Watts.

Gaza: We’ve been invited in for a cup of tea or chai as they call it, but Hassim hed rather fdie than live like this for the rest of his life

George: Derek had an extraordinary enthusiasm for bringing the news. During the crisis following 9/11. I sent Derek with producer Diana Lucas to the Persian Gulf and the mission was to get on to the USS George Washington but getting on to a US warship was no easy feat particularly when you have the likes of BBC and CNN … all the big international channels attempting to do the same thing but Derek and Diana charmed their way on to the USS George Washington now that for me was the extra ordinary determination of Derek.

Derek: A question that comes to mind is how you defend this huge floating platform in a military world of long range missiles which have pin point accuracy and enemy aircraft which are difficult to detect and destroy, we found most of the answers here in the combat directions centre
‘We like to consider ourselves less of a target then an air force base;

George: When he came we got an insight into the magnitude of the American military presence in the Persian Gulf = he brought me the trophy, the trophy was a cap of the USS George Washington which I wear with pride to this day.

Bongani: The very first time I actually saw Derek Watts, Transkei 1982 I am about 8 years old I had never seen a television set before I’m visiting a friend from across the road and it happens to be a Saturday afternoon and Top Sport is on and guess who the presenter was?

Derek: Good Evening, when thirteen wickets tumble in one day you know that the Wanderers track is a little tricky.

V/O
In the early 80’s, Sports-mad Derek was in his dream job, in front of the camera. It’s in Johannesburg presenting Top Sport for SABC.

George: I was a news reader and he was a sports presenter so I didn’t really have a great deal to do with him then, but he came into the agenda offices which was a current affairs show on the SABC to speak to one of my colleagues the anchor of Agenda, John Bishop to ask his advice about coming to a current affairs show Carte Blanche, It’s extraordinary because how did either of us know we would end up working together.

PART 2 Duration: 13mins 40 sec 09 frames ( not counting the 2 sec handles)

V/O
In 1988, M Net, a brand new South African TV channel, launched Carte Blanche …… a weekly current affairs programme.

Ruda: When you think of the beginning of Carte Blanche you must always remember that it was a completely different time. We were the first alternative to the SABC. So August 1988 and Bill Faure phones and he says starting a show an hour on a Sunday night do you want to present?

Archive: First Carte Blanche…Bill Faure announcing name winner

V/O
Carte Blanche was producer Bill Faure’ brain child. He wants Derek to co-host the new show with Ruda. Forty- year old, Derek known as the affable Top Sport presenter, is a surprising choice.

Archive:
Bill Enjoy the programme
Derek: Good evening and welcome to our first edition of Carte Blanche that’s the name that was chosen in our name finding competition…Ruda.

Ruda: I did not know Derek I had never meet him and he came from a completely different background. I came from news and actuality he came from sport. And I think what made the partnership so strong was exactly the fact that we were different.

Ruda: This is a completely different Carte Blanche. We are going to put on a different guise today……..
Derek: Natty little apron
Ruda: Isn’t it just ……..Yes and then what was the middle bit LAUGHS I thought you were going to say it.

Ruda: He was the most amazing partner to have in studio because you could relax completely he would have it in hand and he would never let anything go wrong even if he was teasing me which he did, he would not make me look bad.

Derek: Ruda I am being overcome by these fumes how do you expect me to read my bits.

George: They were a magnificent team together, his Yin to her Yang or whichever way you put it. She was the deeply intellectual serious type and he was the accessible common man. It was a magical combination.

Archive: Up Sound celebration, 95 World Cup,

Ruda: I think he loves being on air, he loves broadcasting and it shines through.

UP SOUND Derek: That was an incredible sight Simon what was it a 6 metre female hey?

Ruda: He has a very quirky sense of humour and he pushes the boundaries he’s not PC. Like the evening we had an insert on fitness of some kind and as we came out of it he said to me on air live, Well women of course keep fit by jumping to conclusions and you know you are just left with what?

Derek: Well jogging through Alex you get a very down to earth look at Alex and the conditions.

V/O
So hard to believe now that this insert on Alexandra Township, in the late 80’s, was a trailblazer.

Ruda: Carte Blanche won the first award ever for an insert on Alexandra township. And It tells you so much about South Africa at that time that it was remarkable because now it wouldn’t be. Then for two white presenters to go and spend a day in Alexandra it won us an award because our white audience had never seen that that…because apartheid worked It kept us apart.

V/O
As in this award-winning story, the magic and personality of what Derek brought to the screen would define all his stories.

Derek: These guys are so tired and in so much pain you want to help them but I guess that’s against the rules.

Claire: You have to tell all different types of stories, and access all parts of you and Derek was able to do that for over 30 years in the ever changing landscape of this country to the homeless person to the Gogo to powerful politicians and business men to crooks …he was able to do it.

Derek: I am walking with Gladys Baloi and she walks quiet well, quiet sprightly really for a dead person because according to Home Affairs she has been dead for five years.

Claire: Derek gave us all the blue print to do the job that we do.

‘We did nothing;
Derek: But the media and most people say the police support Inkatha?
‘That is ridiculous’

Ruda: It was a completely different world that we walked into and which enlarged our world our vision.

V/O
And as South Africa entered a roller coaster ride of change, Carte Blanche held up the mirror in which we saw ourselves.

Derek: Any doubts about the EFF arriving in force were dispelled this morning.

Masa: I remember him covering an EFF rally that was quiet contentious, with farmers on one side and there were racial tensions. He knew how to relate to both sides and make both sides feel they have a friend in him and that will forever be Derek’s legacy. His ability to adapt, his ability to transfer that warmth that he had to everyone and everything he touched

V/O
April 27th 1994: with South Africa’s first democratic elections, the world opened up. As Carte Blanche began to explore outside our borders, Derek’s passport was ready.

Derek: Ma’am Carte Blanche South Africa looking forward to your visit.
Queen: Why Thank you very much.
Derek: Looking forward to seeing you in a couple of weeks time

John: know that Derek had his favourite stories landing on an aircraft carrier in the Gulf War, travelling to Everest Base Camp interviewing Mark Shuttleworth in Russia but for me and maybe what he took for granted is the extent to which his body of work stands out. Just this profound consistency which he was never more or less than Derek Watts that’s what people gravitated towards and it’s a very difficult thing to do in our industry
